He married Jacqueline (Jacquy) Bradnun in 1951 and the following year they emigrated to Britain.  By profession, he was Senior Lecturer in Bantu Studies at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. Ethnomusicology and linguistics were a major part of his life. A multi-instrumentalist, his primary instruments were brasswind (French horn, trumpet and other brasswind instruments including the serpent) and the bassoon. description: Galpin Society Journals, a complete run from 1948-2020, offprints of David Rycroft GSJ articles, GSJ indexes I to XXV (1948-1972), an incomplete run of Galpin Society Newsletters between 2001 and 2011, Historic Brass Society Journall, 1989 to 1995 £300­400 1605-1610 NO LOT ITEMS INHERITED BY DESCENT FROM THE ESTATE OF ARNOLD DOLMETSCH Arnold Dolmetsch was a French-born musician and musical instrument maker who spent much of his working life in England. Born in 1858 in Le Mans, he began his training as a craftsman at his parents’ piano, organ and harmonium factory, Maison Dolmetsch- Guillouard. He studied piano, violin and composition at the Conservatoire royal de Bruxelles and it was here that he ﬁrst encountered musicians playing early musical instruments from the collection belonging to the Conservatoire. In 1883, AD moved to London and enrolled at the Royal College of Music. He was employed as a part-time violin master at Dulwich College and, in his spare time, he started to collect early instruments. He constructed his ﬁrst lute in 1893 and later began building his ﬁrst keyboard instruments. He was active in the cultural life of London and his friends and admirers included William Morris, Edward Burne-Jones, Selwyn Image, Roger Fry, George Bernard Shaw, Marco Pallis, Ezra Pound, George Moore and W.B Yeats. In 1905 he moved with his family to Boston where he built clavichords, harpsichords and viols for Chickering. The family returned to France in 1911 to enable AD to work for Gaveau of Paris. In 1914 he returned to London and, in 1915 his book “The Interpretation of the Music of the XVIIth and XVIIIth Centuries” was published. In 1917, he settled in Haslemere, Surrey. Jesses was the family home, and he established an instrument-making workshop there and proceeded to build copies of almost every kind of instrument dating from the 15th to 18th centuries. He founded an annual chamber music festival which ran from 1925 until 2008. He was largely responsible for the revival of the recorder. In 1938 he was created a chevalier of the Légion d’honneur by the French government.
